Evaluation plan - mixed short-prompt / long-generation LLM serving, scenario variant 145 (system design framing).

0. Scope and non-claims
This is a serving-system measurement plan for one build of one stack. Every number
below is valid only for a fixed (engine commit, model weight hash, quantization,
tokenizer, GPU SKU, driver/CUDA, launch flags) tuple. It says nothing about model
quality, and it does not transfer across engine upgrades or hardware.

1. Workload model (must be pinned before any number is reported)
- Two populations, sampled from a fixed seed: SHORT = input 128-512 tok, output
  16-64 tok; LONG = input 512-2048 tok, output 512-2048 tok. Mix ratio is a
  declared constant (e.g. 70/30) and is reported with every result.
- Generation length must be pinned: set ignore_eos=True with fixed max_tokens per
  population, otherwise output length becomes a random variable and TPOT/P99 drift
  is uninterpretable.
- OPEN-LOOP arrival: Poisson at target request rate. Closed-loop (N fixed workers)
  self-throttles under overload and hides queueing; it may only be used for an
  explicitly labelled saturation-capacity arm.

2. Metric definitions (ambiguity here is the #1 source of bogus comparisons)
- TTFT = first-token timestamp minus request-admit timestamp at the client, and
  separately server-side arrival->first-token. The client-server delta is the
  queue+network component; report both or the queueing claim is unfalsifiable.
- TPOT = (end_to_end - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1), per request, not a global mean.
- Throughput: report output tok/s AND total (prefill+decode) tok/s AND req/s;
  prefill-heavy mixes make total tok/s look good while goodput collapses.
- Goodput = req/s meeting the SLO pair (TTFT <= a, P99 TPOT <= b). This is the
  decision metric; raw throughput is not.
- Queueing: time-in-queue per request, queue depth sampled at >=10 Hz, plus
  preemption/recompute counts from engine metrics.
- Percentiles from raw per-request records only. Never average percentiles across
  runs; pool the samples, then compute.

3. Statistics and warmup
- Discard the first 60 s (or first 200 requests) as warmup: CUDA graph capture,
  autotuning, KV pool growth and clock ramp all land there.
- >=3 independent process restarts per arm; >=1000 requests per arm per population
  so a P99 rests on >=10 tail samples per repeat. Report median-of-runs with
  min/max, and bootstrap CI on P99. If CIs of two arms overlap, the arms are
  NOT distinguishable - say so instead of ranking them.

4. Controlled experiment
- One factor changed per arm; baseline re-measured last to detect drift.
- Environment controls: persistence mode on, locked/recorded clocks, ECC state,
  MPS/MIG off unless under test, no co-tenant on the GPU, NUMA/CPU pinning fixed,
  client on a separate host with headroom verified (client CPU saturation is a
  classic false 'server slowness').

5. Confounders that must be measured, not assumed away
- Thermal/power throttling: log nvidia-smi clocks + throttle reasons throughout.
- KV-cache pressure and preemption: a P99 spike is usually preemption/recompute,
  not compute.
- Chunked prefill / continuous batching interference: long prefills inflate TPOT of
  in-flight decodes; this is expected, quantify it, do not call it a regression
  without the prefill-token timeline.
- Tokenizer differences changing effective token counts between arms.
- Client-side coordinated omission: use scheduled send times, not send-after-reply.

6. Rollback / decision gates (declare before running)
- Ship only if goodput improves >= 10 percent with P99 TTFT and P99 TPOT no worse
  than 5 percent, on >=3 repeats, with non-overlapping CIs.
- Roll back on: P99 TTFT regression > 20 percent, any OOM/preempt-rate increase
  > 2x, error rate > 0.1 percent, or unreproducible results across restarts.
- Canary at <=5 percent traffic for 24 h before fleet rollout; keep the previous
  container image pinned for one-command revert.

7. Falsifiable hypothesis (design arm)
H0: at the 70/30 short/long mix, disaggregating prefill and decode onto separate
replica pools does NOT improve goodput by more than 10 percent versus a single
co-located continuous-batching pool at equal total GPU count.
H1: it does, because decode-phase TPOT is currently degraded by long prefill chunks
sharing the same scheduler step.
Discriminating measurement: per-step timeline of prefill tokens vs decode tokens,
and TPOT conditioned on 'a long prefill was co-scheduled in the same step'. If TPOT
inflation under co-scheduling is < 5 percent, H1 is refuted and disaggregation
(which adds KV transfer cost over the interconnect) is not justified. Cross-node KV
transfer for a disaggregated design must itself be budgeted: measure the KV bytes
per request and the achieved RDMA bandwidth, and confirm transfer time < the TTFT
budget you are trying to protect.

8. Reporting artifact
One table per arm: config hash, mix, arrival rate, req count, warmup
excluded, TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, output tok/s, goodput,
queue-wait p99, preempt count, peak KV utilization, clock/throttle log.
Raw per-request records are archived alongside; any claim not derivable
from those records is withdrawn.
risks: source_assistant is a grading rubric, not an answer; training on it teaches meta-commentary ('answer should state...') instead of engineering reasoning
no metric definitions, no arrival model and no sample-size rule, so any P99 produced from it is not decision-grade
unpinned generation length and closed-loop load generation would silently invalidate TPOT and tail-latency comparisons
no rollback threshold or canary step, so the plan cannot gate a production change
evidence_required: engine commit, model weight hash, quantization, tokenizer and full launch flags for every arm
raw per-request traces: queue wait, client and server TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end, output token count
engine metrics: KV-cache utilization, queue depth, preemption/recompute counts, batch composition per step
nvidia-smi clock, power and throttle-reason timeline plus persistence/ECC/MIG state
client-side headroom evidence (CPU, network) proving the load generator was not the bottleneck
>=3 independent restarts per arm with bootstrap CIs on P99

source_user: A service receives a mix of short prompts and long generations. Design an evaluation plan that reports TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, and P99 latency. Scenario variant 155: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.

corrected_answer:
Evaluation plan - mixed short-prompt / long-generation LLM serving, scenario variant 155 (troubleshooting framing).

0. Scope and non-claims
This is a serving-system measurement plan for one build of one stack. Every number
below is valid only for a fixed (engine commit, model weight hash, quantization,
tokenizer, GPU SKU, driver/CUDA, launch flags) tuple. It says nothing about model
quality, and it does not transfer across engine upgrades or hardware.

1. Workload model (must be pinned before any number is reported)
- Two populations, sampled from a fixed seed: SHORT = input 128-512 tok, output
  16-64 tok; LONG = input 512-2048 tok, output 512-2048 tok. Mix ratio is a
  declared constant (e.g. 70/30) and is reported with every result.
- Generation length must be pinned: set ignore_eos=True with fixed max_tokens per
  population, otherwise output length becomes a random variable and TPOT/P99 drift
  is uninterpretable.
- OPEN-LOOP arrival: Poisson at target request rate. Closed-loop (N fixed workers)
  self-throttles under overload and hides queueing; it may only be used for an
  explicitly labelled saturation-capacity arm.

2. Metric definitions (ambiguity here is the #1 source of bogus comparisons)
- TTFT = first-token timestamp minus request-admit timestamp at the client, and
  separately server-side arrival->first-token. The client-server delta is the
  queue+network component; report both or the queueing claim is unfalsifiable.
- TPOT = (end_to_end - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1), per request, not a global mean.
- Throughput: report output tok/s AND total (prefill+decode) tok/s AND req/s;
  prefill-heavy mixes make total tok/s look good while goodput collapses.
- Goodput = req/s meeting the SLO pair (TTFT <= a, P99 TPOT <= b). This is the
  decision metric; raw throughput is not.
- Queueing: time-in-queue per request, queue depth sampled at >=10 Hz, plus
  preemption/recompute counts from engine metrics.
- Percentiles from raw per-request records only. Never average percentiles across
  runs; pool the samples, then compute.

3. Statistics and warmup
- Discard the first 60 s (or first 200 requests) as warmup: CUDA graph capture,
  autotuning, KV pool growth and clock ramp all land there.
- >=3 independent process restarts per arm; >=1000 requests per arm per population
  so a P99 rests on >=10 tail samples per repeat. Report median-of-runs with
  min/max, and bootstrap CI on P99. If CIs of two arms overlap, the arms are
  NOT distinguishable - say so instead of ranking them.

4. Controlled experiment
- One factor changed per arm; baseline re-measured last to detect drift.
- Environment controls: persistence mode on, locked/recorded clocks, ECC state,
  MPS/MIG off unless under test, no co-tenant on the GPU, NUMA/CPU pinning fixed,
  client on a separate host with headroom verified (client CPU saturation is a
  classic false 'server slowness').

5. Confounders that must be measured, not assumed away
- Thermal/power throttling: log nvidia-smi clocks + throttle reasons throughout.
- KV-cache pressure and preemption: a P99 spike is usually preemption/recompute,
  not compute.
- Chunked prefill / continuous batching interference: long prefills inflate TPOT of
  in-flight decodes; this is expected, quantify it, do not call it a regression
  without the prefill-token timeline.
- Tokenizer differences changing effective token counts between arms.
- Client-side coordinated omission: use scheduled send times, not send-after-reply.

6. Rollback / decision gates (declare before running)
- Ship only if goodput improves >= 10 percent with P99 TTFT and P99 TPOT no worse
  than 5 percent, on >=3 repeats, with non-overlapping CIs.
- Roll back on: P99 TTFT regression > 20 percent, any OOM/preempt-rate increase
  > 2x, error rate > 0.1 percent, or unreproducible results across restarts.
- Canary at <=5 percent traffic for 24 h before fleet rollout; keep the previous
  container image pinned for one-command revert.

7. Falsifiable hypothesis (diagnosis arm)
H0: the observed P99 latency tail is caused by admission queueing at overload, not
by per-token compute slowdown.
H1 (alternative): the tail is caused by KV-cache exhaustion triggering preemption
and prefill recompute.
Discriminating measurement: for tail requests, decompose end-to-end into queue wait,
TTFT-minus-queue, and decode time. If queue wait dominates (>60 percent of the
excess), it is admission/capacity - fix with rate limiting or replicas. If decode
time and preemption counters spike together while queue wait is flat, it is KV
pressure - fix with max_num_seqs / KV block budget / shorter max_model_len. If
neither moves but clocks drop, it is thermal. These three predict disjoint counter
signatures, so exactly one survives.

8. Reporting artifact
One table per arm: config hash, mix, arrival rate, req count, warmup
excluded, TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, output tok/s, goodput,
queue-wait p99, preempt count, peak KV utilization, clock/throttle log.
Raw per-request records are archived alongside; any claim not derivable
from those records is withdrawn.
risks: source_assistant is a grading rubric, not an answer; training on it teaches meta-commentary ('answer should state...') instead of engineering reasoning
no metric definitions, no arrival model and no sample-size rule, so any P99 produced from it is not decision-grade
unpinned generation length and closed-loop load generation would silently invalidate TPOT and tail-latency comparisons
no rollback threshold or canary step, so the plan cannot gate a production change
